question.text:
Consider the relation $R$ defined on the set $A = \{\mu, \nu, \rho, \lambda, \phi\}$ as \[ R = \big\{ (\nu,\nu), (\lambda,\lambda), (\phi,\phi) \big\}. \]

Select the options that make the following reasoning correct:
question.explanation:
First, recall the following definitions:

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is symmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (y,x) \in R. \] In other words, if a pair $(x,y)$ belongs to a symmetric relation, then the pair $(y,x)$ should also be in the relation.

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is antisymmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \quad\textrm{and}\quad (y,x) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\quad x=y. \] In other words, only one of the pairs, either $(x,y)$ or $(y,x),$ can be in an antisymmetric relation. Note that this condition allows pairs of the form $(x,x).$

Our relation is defined on $\{\alpha, \beta, \delta, \gamma\},$ and has no pairs of the form $(x,y)$ with $x \neq y.$ As a result, the propositions in both implications above are false. Hence, the implications themselves must be true. Therefore, since for all $x,y \in A,$ we have

\begin{align*} \require{cancel} (x,y)\in R & \qquad \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\Longrightarrow} \qquad (y,x)\in R, \\[5pt] (x,y) \in R \quad\textrm{and}\quad (y,x) \in R & \qquad \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\Longrightarrow} \qquad x=y, \end{align*} the relation is $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{both symmetric and antisymmetric}}.$

question.text: Which of the above digraphs represents a relation, defined on the set $A = \{\alpha,\beta,\delta\},$ that is neither symmetric nor antisymmetric?
question.explanation:
First, recall the following definitions:

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is symmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (y,x) \in R. \] In terms of a digraph, if we have an arrow $x \rightarrow y,$ then the arrow $y \rightarrow x$ must be in the digraph too.

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is antisymmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \quad\textrm{and}\quad (y,x) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\quad x=y. \] So, only one of the arrows, either $x \rightarrow y$ or $y \rightarrow x,$ can be in the digraph of an antisymmetric relation. Note that this condition allows loops.

With that in mind, let's examine our digraphs.

  • Digraph I represents an antisymmetric relation since for all possible $x$ and $y$ with $x \neq y,$ at most one of the arrows (either $x \rightarrow y$ or $y \rightarrow x,$ but not both) belongs to the digraph.

  • Digraph II represents neither a symmetric nor an antisymmetric relation. It's not symmetric since the arrow $\delta \rightarrow \alpha$ belongs to the digraph while the arrow $\alpha \rightarrow \delta$ does not. It is not antisymmetric since, for example, arrows $\beta \rightarrow \delta$ and $\delta \rightarrow \beta$ belong to the digraph.

  • Digraph III represents a symmetric relation since for every arrow $x \rightarrow y$ belonging to the graph, the corresponding inverse arrow $y \rightarrow x$ also belongs to the graph.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

question.text: Which of the plots above represents a relation defined on the set $A=\{\alpha, \beta, \delta\}$ that is both symmetric and antisymmetric?
question.explanation:
First, recall the following definitions:

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is symmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (y,x) \in R. \] In terms of a plot, if a point $(x,y)$ belongs to the plot, then $(y,x),$ the point symmetric to $(x,y)$ over the diagonal line $y=x,$ should also be on the plot.

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is antisymmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \quad\textrm{and}\quad (y,x) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\quad x=y. \] So, only one of the points, either $(x,y)$ or $(y,x),$ can be on the plot of an antisymmetric relation. Note that this condition allows points on the diagonal line $y=x.$

With that in mind, let's draw the diagonal line $y=x$ and examine our plots.

  • Plot I represents a relation that is both symmetric and antisymmetric. Notice that it has no pairs of the form $(x,y)$ with $x \neq y.$ As a result, the propositions in both implications above are false. Hence, the implications themselves must be true.

  • Plot II represents an antisymmetric relation since the plot contains at most one point from each pair of the points symmetric over the line $y = x.$

  • Plot III represents a symmetric relation since the plot is symmetric over the line $y = x.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

  • Plot I represents a symmetric relation since the plot is symmetric over the line $y=x.$

  • Plot II represents an antisymmetric relation since the plot contains at most one point from each pair of the points symmetric over the line $y=x.$

  • Plot III represents neither a symmetric nor an antisymmetric relation. It's not symmetric since, for example, the pair $(4,2)$ belongs to the plot while the point $(2,4)$ does not. And it's not antisymmetric since it contains the pairs $(0,4)$ and $(4,0).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

question.text:
Let $R$ be a relation defined on the set $\mathbb{R}$ as follows:

$x \, R \, y$ if and only if $x^2 - y^2 = 0$

Select the options that make the following reasoning correct:
question.explanation:
First, recall the following definitions:

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is symmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (y,x) \in R. \] In other words, if a pair $(x,y)$ belongs to a symmetric relation, then the pair $(y,x)$ should also be in the relation.

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is antisymmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \quad\textrm{and}\quad (y,x) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\quad x=y. \] In other words, only one of the pairs, either $(x,y)$ or $(y,x),$ can be in an antisymmetric relation. Note that this condition allows pairs of the form $(x,x).$

The relation $R$ is symmetric. Indeed, for any real numbers $x$ and $y,$ if $x^2 - y^2 = 0,$ then $y^2 - x^2 = 0.$

Therefore, we can conclude the following:

Since for all $x,y \in \mathbb{R},$ we have \[ \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}x^2 - y^2 = 0} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}y^2 - x^2 = 0}, \] the relation is $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{symmetric}}.$

Note: $R$ is not antisymmetric since, for example, $1^2 - (-1)^2 = 0$ and $(-1)^2 - 1^2 = 0$ but $1 \neq -1.$

question.text:
Let $R$ be a relation defined on the set $\mathbb{R}$ as follows:

$x \, R \, y$ if and only if $x \leq y$

Select the options that make the following reasoning correct:
question.explanation:
First, recall the following definitions:

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is symmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (y,x) \in R. \] In other words, if a pair $(x,y)$ belongs to a symmetric relation, then the pair $(y,x)$ should also be in the relation.

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is antisymmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \quad\textrm{and}\quad (y,x) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\quad x=y. \] In other words, only one of the pairs, either $(x,y)$ or $(y,x),$ can be in an antisymmetric relation. Note that this condition allows pairs of the form $(x,x).$

The relation $R$ is antisymmetric. Indeed, for any real numbers $x$ and $y,$ if $x \leq y$ and $y \leq x,$ then $x$ and $y$ must be the same number.

Therefore, we can conclude the following:

Since for all $x,y \in \mathbb{R},$ we have \[ \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}x \leq y \quad\textrm{and}\quad y \leq x} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}x = y}, \] the relation is $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{antisymmetric}}.$

Note: $R$ is not symmetric since, for example, $0 \leq 1$ but $1 \not\leq 0.$

question.text:
Which of the following relations are antisymmetric?

  • $x \: R \: y$ if and only if $x \geq y,$ defined on $\mathbb{R}$

  • $x \: S \: y$ if and only if $x \equiv y \: (\textrm{mod}\:5),$ defined on $\mathbb{Z}$

  • $x \: T \: y$ if and only if $|x| = |y|,$ defined on $\mathbb{R}$
question.explanation:
First, recall the following definitions:

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is symmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (y,x) \in R. \] In other words, if a pair $(x,y)$ belongs to a symmetric relation, then the pair $(y,x)$ should also be in the relation.

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is antisymmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \quad\textrm{and}\quad (y,x) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\quad x=y. \] In other words, only one of the pairs, either $(x,y)$ or $(y,x),$ can be in an antisymmetric relation. Note that this condition allows pairs of the form $(x,x).$

With that in mind, let's examine our relations.

  • Relation $R$ is antisymmetric. Indeed, if $(x,y) \in R$ and $(y,x) \in R,$ then $x = y.$ Notice that \[ x \geq y \quad \textrm{and} \quad y \geq x \qquad \Longrightarrow\qquad x = y \] for all $x,y \in \mathbb{R}.$

  • Relation $S$ is not antisymmetric. Notice that

    • $(1,6) \in S$ since $1 \equiv 6 \: (\textrm{mod}\:5),$ and

    • $(6,1) \in S$ since $6 \equiv 1 \: (\textrm{mod}\:5).$

  • Relation $T$ is not antisymmetric. Notice that

    • $(-1,1) \in T$ since $|-1| = |1|,$ and

    • $(1,-1) \in T$ since $|1| = |-1|.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$R$ only."

question.text:
Which of the following relations are antisymmetric?

  • $x \: R \: y$ if and only if $5 \mid xy,$ defined on $\mathbb{Z}$

  • $x \: S \: y$ if and only if $x - y \lt 8,$ defined on $\mathbb{N}$

  • $X \: T \: Y$ if and only if $X \subseteq Y,$ defined on $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})$
question.explanation:
First, recall the following definitions:

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is symmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (y,x) \in R. \] In other words, if a pair $(x,y)$ belongs to a symmetric relation, then the pair $(y,x)$ should also be in the relation.

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is antisymmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \quad\textrm{and}\quad (y,x) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\quad x=y. \] In other words, only one of the pairs, either $(x,y)$ or $(y,x),$ can be in an antisymmetric relation. Note that this condition allows pairs of the form $(x,x).$

With that in mind, let's examine our relations.

  • Relation $R$ is not antisymmetric. Notice that

    • $(1,5) \in R$ since $5 \mid (1 \cdot 5),$ and

    • $(5,1) \in R$ since $5 \mid (5 \cdot 1).$

  • Relation $S$ is not antisymmetric. Notice that

    • $(1,3) \in S$ since $3 - 1 \lt 8,$ and

    • $(3,1) \in S$ since $1 - 3 \lt 8.$

  • Relation $T$ is antisymmetric. Indeed, if $(X,Y) \in T$ and $(Y,X) \in T,$ then $X = Y.$ Notice that \[ X \subseteq Y \quad \textrm{and} \quad Y \subseteq X \qquad \Longrightarrow\qquad X = Y \] for all $X, Y \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$T$ only."

question.text:
Which of the following relations are symmetric?

  • $x \: R \: y$ if and only if $y = x^2,$ defined on $\mathbb{R}$

  • $X \: S \: Y$ if and only if $X \subset Y,$ defined on $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})$

  • $x \: T \: y$ if and only if $4 \mid (x+y),$ defined on $\mathbb{N}$
question.explanation:
First, recall the following definitions:

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is symmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (y,x) \in R. \] In other words, if a pair $(x,y)$ belongs to a symmetric relation, then the pair $(y,x)$ should also be in the relation.

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is antisymmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \quad\textrm{and}\quad (y,x) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\quad x=y. \] In other words, only one of the pairs, either $(x,y)$ or $(y,x),$ can be in an antisymmetric relation. Note that this condition allows pairs of the form $(x,x).$

With that in mind, let's examine our relations.

  • Relation $R$ is not symmetric. Notice that

    • $(-1,1) \in R$ since $1 = (-1)^2,$ while

    • $(1,-1) \notin R$ since $-1 \neq 1^2.$

  • Relation $S$ is not symmetric. Notice that

    • $(\{1\},\mathbb{Z}) \in S$ since $\{1\} \subset \mathbb{Z},$ while

    • $(\mathbb{Z},\{1\}) \notin S$ since $\mathbb{Z} \not\subset \{1\}.$

  • Relation $T$ is symmetric. Indeed, if $(x,y) \in T$ then $(y,x) \in T.$ Notice that \[ 4 \mid (x+y) \qquad \Longrightarrow\qquad 4 \mid (y+x) \] for all $x,y \in \mathbb{N}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$T$ only."
